titles.l3: What the counting numbers can do

kernelIdea: ℤ is closed under addition, additive inverses, and multiplication, and satisfies the distributive law — this makes it a ring. It is not closed under multiplicative inverses: only 1 and −1 have integer reciprocals.

kernels.l1: Adding whole piles keeps them whole. Sharing them out does not.
kernels.l2: Adding and multiplying whole numbers always gives you back a whole number. Dividing can throw you out of the whole numbers altogether.
kernels.l3: The counting numbers are closed under adding and multiplying — those never take you outside. Subtracting and dividing can, and those two gaps are where new numbers come from.
kernels.l4: The integers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, and multiplication distributes over addition. They are not closed under division: only 1 and −1 have integer reciprocals.
kernels.l5: Closure under addition, subtraction and multiplication, plus distributivity, is the standard list of arithmetic rules. What the integers lack is reciprocals — and that absence is the whole subject of §4.5.
kernels.l6: The integers obey a standard list of arithmetic rules, and so do polynomials and square grids of numbers — which is why collecting the rules is worth doing. Later courses give the list a name.
kernels.l7: The integers are closed under addition, negation and multiplication and obey the distributive law; only 1 and −1 have reciprocals. That last failure is the one that matters, and §4.5 repairs it.
kernels.l8: ℤ is an integral domain whose units are ±1; the ring axioms are exactly the properties used in every integer proof, and abstraction of them is the starting point of algebra.
